recaps.in_short: Carter Bennett leaves Green Creek alone to follow Gavin, travelling without pack bonds in a way that steadily wears a wolf down. He finds him, and the two are caught by hunters who trap and cage wolves; they escape together, and Gavin, who has spent years unable to hold human form, begins to be a man again. On the road back, Carter learns how much of his family's history his father kept from him, including what was done to Gavin and how the Bennett line is bound up with Robert Livingstone's ruin. In Green Creek the pack has to accept Livingstone's son among them, hardest of all for Gordo. Livingstone's plan finally comes into the open, and the pack meets it together. He is killed, the threat that has hung over the Bennetts across four books ends with him, and Carter and Gavin become mates. The pack closes the series intact and at home: Ox and Joe as alphas, Gordo and Mark, Kelly and Robbie, Carter and Gavin, with Green Creek finally safe.

recaps.text: Previously: Ox Matheson was taken in as a boy by the Bennett werewolves of Green Creek, Oregon, and claimed by their youngest son Joe. When the rogue alpha Richard Collins killed Thomas Bennett, Joe inherited his power and left with his brothers Carter and Kelly and the pack witch Gordo Livingstone to hunt Richard; Ox held together everyone who stayed and became an alpha himself. Richard was killed in Green Creek, at the cost of Ox's mother's life, and a traitor inside the wolf leadership was exposed. Ox and Joe now lead the pack as mates. Gordo's father, Robert Livingstone, a witch stripped of his magic and exiled by Thomas decades ago, proved to be alive and carrying stolen alpha power. He sent Omegas against Green Creek, escaped Gordo, and took Robbie Fontaine, erasing every memory Robbie had of the pack. The Bennetts went into the leadership's seat at Caswell and brought Robbie home, and his memories returned; he and Kelly are mates, and Gordo and Mark are mates. In the course of it the pack met Gavin, a wolf who could not take human form, who turned out to be Robert Livingstone's son and Gordo's half-brother. Gavin left Green Creek, and Carter went after him alone.

Carter Bennett is on the road, chasing a trail that keeps going cold. He has left Green Creek without telling anyone what he intended and without his alphas, and being cut off from his pack bonds does to a wolf exactly what everyone warned him it would: it wears at his control and at his sense of himself, a little more each week. He hides how bad it is getting, from his family on the phone and from himself. Along the way he thinks about what it has meant to be the eldest Bennett brother, the one who makes the jokes so that nobody has to look at how frightened everyone is, and how comprehensively that has stopped working. He is looking for Gavin, who left because being Robert Livingstone's son inside Gordo Livingstone's pack had no comfortable shape, and Carter is not able to explain, even to himself, why he could not let that stand.

Carter finds Gavin, and almost immediately both of them are taken. Hunters, humans who trap and cage wolves and treat them as animals or as merchandise, have them, and Carter learns how much organization stands behind an operation the packs have preferred not to look at. He and Gavin get out together, and being locked up alongside each other forces a bluntness neither has managed before. Gavin has spent years unable to hold human form, and his shape and his speech both come back to him unevenly; what he says when he can speak is direct, unsoftened and frequently more honest than Carter is ready for. They start moving west, hunted, on foot and by whatever they can beg or take, with Carter's isolation from his pack getting steadily more dangerous.

On the way back Carter finds out how much of his own family's history was withheld from him. His father Thomas made decisions decades ago whose consequences the pack is still paying: what was done to Robert Livingstone and why, what became of Livingstone's other son, and how far the Bennett line's power and Livingstone's ruin are bound together. Carter has to hold those revelations without an alpha to steady him, and he is angry in a way he has never allowed himself to be about his father, his brothers and his own habit of absorbing everything so no one else has to. Gavin, who has been the object of most of these decisions rather than a party to them, is the person Carter says it to. What is between them stops being deniable.

Carter and Gavin reach Green Creek, and the reunion is not simple: the pack is relieved, furious and wary all at once, and having Robert Livingstone's son living in the house is hardest of all on Gordo, whose entire life has been built against his father. Elizabeth, Ox and Joe make room anyway. What the pack has learned about the hunters, and what Carter has learned about his father, both have to be put in front of everyone, and the wolf leadership in Caswell under Michelle Hughes proves to be neither able nor especially willing to help. Robert Livingstone's purpose finally comes into the open, and it is bigger than revenge on the Bennetts. The pack stops waiting to be attacked and starts preparing to end it.

The confrontation with Robert Livingstone comes, and he is everything the pack feared: a witch with alpha power, Omegas at his command, and a willingness to use his own sons against each other. The fighting is costly and the pack meets it as one, wolves, witch and humans together, with Ox and Joe leading and Gordo and Gavin each forced to face what their father is directly. Carter, who has spent the book believing he is the one the family can most afford to lose, ends up in the middle of it.

Robert Livingstone is killed, and the threat that has hung over Green Creek since before Carter was born ends with him; the Omegas and the machinery he built do not outlast him. The pack survives, and afterward it does the slow work of burying what needs burying and repairing what can be repaired. Carter and Gavin become mates, and Carter finally stops being only the brother who holds everyone else up. Gavin, who was his father's creation and then his father's abandoned son, is a Bennett wolf because the pack chooses him. Green Creek is safe, the leadership in Caswell no longer holds any authority over the Bennetts, and the secrets Thomas Bennett kept have been dealt with rather than handed down again. The series closes with the whole pack at home, paired off and whole, looking forward.

characters.description: The narrator, now leading what is left of the Reckoners in practice if not in title. He is committed to a position most of the organisation considers reckless: that Epics are driven to cruelty by fear rather than by the power itself, that facing that fear can undo it, and that the man who founded the Reckoners can therefore be recovered rather than killed. He still keeps notebooks, still produces terrible metaphors, and is increasingly interested in where Epic powers actually come from.
characters.name: David Charleston

characters.description: An Epic who returns to life after being killed and who can briefly pull objects and people across from other versions of reality. She learned to use her abilities by confronting what frightens her instead of avoiding it, which makes her the living proof of David's argument and the model for everything he intends to try. She is with the Reckoners and with David, and she is far more realistic than he is about what the plan will cost.
characters.name: Megan

characters.description: The founder of the Reckoners: an Epic whose powers grant forcefields, healing and the transmutation of matter, and who lent them to his team through equipment for years rather than use them himself. He gave in to the corruption that comes with using Epic power and is now one of the most dangerous Epics alive, with a complete knowledge of every Reckoner method because he invented them. David refuses to treat him as beyond saving.
characters.name: Prof

characters.description: The Reckoners' intelligence specialist and the person who has known Prof longest. She keeps the records, plans the operations, and has the hardest time of anyone on the team with what he has become.
characters.name: Tia

characters.description: The team's sniper: a Tennessean with an unverifiable claim to Scottish ancestry, a limitless supply of tall stories, and complete steadiness when it matters.
characters.name: Cody

characters.description: The team's weapons and demolitions specialist, calm and deliberate, and one of the Faithful, who have always expected an Epic to appear who protects people rather than ruling them. Recent events have made his position considerably less eccentric than it used to sound.
characters.name: Abraham

characters.description: The youngest Reckoner, recruited in Babilar: a demolitions specialist who talks constantly, adapts quickly and is still learning how much the work costs.
characters.name: Mizzy

characters.description: The maker who supplies the Reckoners' technology, working out of a fortified foundry. He is almost completely paralysed and speaks through a machine, he is not interested in helping anyone for free, and the devices he builds run on components harvested from the bodies of dead Epics.
characters.name: Knighthawk

characters.description: A High Epic who takes other Epics' abilities for himself simply by being near them, which makes him effectively unassailable and enormously powerful. He nominally rules Ildithia and has no interest whatsoever in ruling it: he is sullen, idle and impossible to threaten or bargain with.
characters.name: Larcener

characters.description: An Epic who accumulates heat, releases it in city-destroying quantities, and moves himself instantly from place to place. He survived Babilar and believes the destruction of humanity is a duty laid on him, which he pursues courteously and without any particular malice.
characters.name: Obliteration

characters.description: The red star that appeared in the sky on the night the first Epics gained their powers and has hung there ever since, and the source of every Epic ability in the world. It proves to be a being rather than an object.
characters.name: Calamity

recaps.ending: David reaches Calamity itself and finds that it is a being rather than a star: an entity from outside this world that came here and gave people powers, and whose gift carries with it the compulsion toward cruelty that has ruined nearly everyone who received it. Larcener proves to be another of the same kind, an earlier arrival who has been living among humans. David confronts Calamity, refuses the terms it offers him, and forces it to leave, which ends its hold over the world. Prof is recovered rather than killed: stripped of what was driving him, he is himself again, and the founder of the Reckoners is returned to them, though not undamaged by what he did while he was gone. David does not come through unchanged either, and ends the book with abilities of his own, which makes him precisely the kind of creature he spent his life hunting and the first test of his own argument that an Epic can choose otherwise. The Reckoners are left in a world that still contains Epics but no longer contains the force that made them monstrous, facing the work of rebuilding rather than the work of resisting.
recaps.in_short: Prof has fallen and taken a city, and the surviving Reckoners are fugitives. David's position is now the team's working theory: Epics are driven to cruelty by fear rather than by power, and facing that fear can undo it, with Megan as the proof. They track Prof to Ildithia, the remains of Atlanta, a city built of salt that crumbles at one edge and regrows at the other so the whole thing migrates across the country. Operating under cover, short of equipment and dependent on the maker Knighthawk, they try to reach a man who invented every method they use against him, while the power-stealing Epic Larcener attaches himself to them and the city-destroying Obliteration pursues his own plan. David's investigation into the origin of Epic powers points at Calamity itself, and he finds a way to reach it. Calamity proves to be a being that came here and gave out powers, and Larcener is another of the same kind. David forces Calamity to withdraw, Prof is freed and restored, and David ends the book an Epic himself.

recaps.text: Previously: a red star called Calamity appeared and ordinary people began gaining superhuman powers, almost all of them using those powers to rule or destroy. David Charleston joined the Reckoners, the only organisation that assassinates Epics, and helped kill Steelheart, who had turned Chicago to steel and ruled it for a decade. He learned that the Reckoners' leader, Prof, is himself an Epic whose forcefield, healing and matter-transmuting powers were lent to the team through equipment, and that his teammate Megan is an Epic who returns from death and can briefly pull people and objects out of other versions of reality. In Babilar, the flooded ruin of Manhattan, the dying High Epic Regalia manoeuvred Prof into using his powers under extreme emotional pressure so that he would fall to the corruption they carry, and he did. Megan, meanwhile, learned to use her abilities without being corrupted, by facing her fears instead of avoiding them. Prof broke with the Reckoners and left, and David resolved to reclaim him rather than kill him.

Prof, fallen and fully corrupted, has taken control of a city, and the Reckoners who are left, David, Megan, Tia, Cody, Abraham and Mizzy, are fugitives without a base or a supply line. David's argument has become the team's operating theory: that Epics are driven to cruelty by fear rather than by the power itself, and that confronting that fear can reverse it, with Megan as the standing proof. Their objective is therefore not to kill Prof but to reclaim him, which most of the surviving organisation regards as sentimental and likely to get people killed. Tracking him leads the team to Ildithia, the remains of Atlanta, a city continuously rebuilt out of salt: it crumbles at one edge and regrows at the other, so the whole city slowly migrates across the landscape.

The team establishes itself in Ildithia under cover, learning a city where the buildings dissolve on a schedule and everything has to be rebuilt weekly. It is nominally ruled by Larcener, a High Epic who absorbs the abilities of any Epic near him and who cannot be bothered to govern anything. The Reckoners are badly short of equipment, and the only source is Knighthawk, the maker who has always supplied them: a man who is almost entirely paralysed, uninterested in helping them, and whose devices are built from components taken out of dead Epics. David also has to face the team's real objection to his plan, which is that trying to save Prof rather than kill him is a risk the survivors will pay for.

Prof arrives in Ildithia and takes it, displacing Larcener, who attaches himself to the Reckoners instead and proves to be as unhelpful in their base as he was in his palace. The team is now operating inside a city held by the man they intend to rescue, against an opponent who knows every Reckoner tactic, item of equipment and habit because he devised them. David works on how to force an Epic to confront the fear their power feeds on, using Megan's experience as the template, and looks for a way to weaken Prof enough to get near him. Obliteration, who survived Babilar, is also in the city, pursuing a purpose of his own.

The Reckoners' operations against Prof are expensive. He anticipates them, and the team's losses are severe enough that the argument over whether he can be redeemed turns bitter. David pushes further into the question he has been circling since Babilar, which is where Epic powers actually come from, and the answer keeps pointing back at Calamity itself, the red star that appeared on the night the first Epics manifested. Knighthawk's technology, which is built out of Epic remains and grants borrowed abilities to ordinary people, turns out to say more about the nature of those powers than anything the Reckoners have studied.

Prof's grip on Ildithia tightens and the Reckoners are forced further into the open, while Obliteration's own plan for the city runs alongside everything else. Working from what Knighthawk's devices imply about Epic bodies and from what Megan can do with other versions of reality, David concludes that Calamity is not a phenomenon but a source, and that it can be reached and confronted directly. The team, short of people and of options, commits to a plan built on that conclusion instead of on any conventional assassination.

The confrontation with Prof comes to a head in Ildithia, with David committing to the only version of the plan that could work: not killing him, but forcing him into a position where he must face the fear his power is built on, the same way Megan faced hers. At the same time David goes through with reaching Calamity itself, on the reasoning that whatever gave out these powers can also take them back, and that everything about the last decade follows from what Calamity actually is.

David reaches Calamity and finds a being rather than a star: an entity from outside this world that came here and gave people powers, and whose gift carries the compulsion toward cruelty that ruined nearly everyone who took it. Larcener proves to be one of the same kind, an earlier arrival hiding among humans. David confronts Calamity, refuses what it offers him, and forces it to leave, ending its hold on the world. Prof is recovered rather than killed: freed of what was driving him, he is himself again and returns to the Reckoners, though marked by what he did. David is changed too, ending the book with abilities of his own, which makes him the sort of creature he spent his life hunting and the first real test of his own argument that an Epic can choose otherwise. The Reckoners are left in a world that still has Epics but no longer has the thing that made them monstrous, with rebuilding rather than resistance ahead of them.

characters.description: A four-year-old girl living on Ganymede, the agricultural moon that feeds the outer planets. She has a genetic immune disorder that requires regular treatment and frequent clinic visits, and she is collected from her daycare by her doctor on an ordinary morning.
characters.name: Mei Meng

characters.description: Mei's physician on Ganymede, familiar to the children in his care and trusted by their parents, who arrives at her daycare to take her for a scheduled appointment.
characters.name: Doctor Strickland

characters.description: A gunnery sergeant in the Martian Marine Corps, very tall and heavily built even for a Martian, serving on the tense demilitarized line between the Martian and United Nations garrisons on Ganymede. She is a career soldier who loves the work, trusts her platoon, and has no interest in politics until the day her patrol is destroyed by something that should not exist.
characters.name: Roberta Draper

characters.description: Captain of the Rocinante, working under contract to Fred Johnson and the Outer Planets Alliance, hunting pirates and enforcing order in the Belt. Roughly a year and a half after Eros, the openness that once defined him has hardened: he shoots earlier, tells the public less, and is uneasy about who he is becoming.
characters.name: James Holden

characters.description: The Rocinante's executive officer and engineer, a Belter whose steadiness holds the crew together and who is the one person willing to tell Holden plainly that he is changing for the worse.
characters.name: Naomi Nagata

characters.description: The Rocinante's mechanic, an Earther with a placid manner and an entirely practical view of violence, who takes his sense of right and wrong from the people he has chosen rather than from any principle of his own.
characters.name: Amos Burton

characters.description: The Rocinante's pilot, a former Martian navy flyer with a Mariner Valley drawl, cheerfully talkative and among the best ship handlers alive.
characters.name: Alex Kamal

characters.description: Head of the Outer Planets Alliance's operation at Tycho Station and the Rocinante's employer, a former UN colonel trying to turn a loose movement into a legitimate government while Earth and Mars look for reasons to treat it as a criminal one.
characters.name: Fred Johnson

characters.description: A botanist on Ganymede specializing in engineered crops for the moon's domes, precise, mild and easily lost in technical detail. He is divorced and shares custody of his daughter Mei, and when the fighting starts he discovers she was taken from her daycare hours earlier by her doctor. Without her medication she will not survive long, and he goes on looking for her after everyone else has stopped.
characters.name: Praxidike Meng

characters.description: A senior official in the United Nations government on Earth, an elderly woman with grandchildren, an indulgent husband and a vocabulary that startles admirals. She has spent a long career reading what people are not saying, and she is certain that the shooting on Ganymede was provoked and that someone inside her own government arranged it.
characters.name: Chrisjen Avasarala

characters.description: Avasarala's superior in the United Nations government, a smooth and effective political operator who shares her hawkishness about Mars and appears to be her closest ally in managing the crisis.
characters.name: Sadavir Errinwright

characters.description: A wealthy Luna industrialist, father of the Julie Mao who died on Eros, who withdrew from public life after the protomolecule experiment was exposed. Avasarala's investigation keeps returning to his companies as the only private hands with the money, ships and laboratories to have continued that work.
characters.name: Jules-Pierre Mao

characters.description: A United Nations admiral with a hard line on Mars and the Belt, impatient with diplomacy and openly contemptuous of civilian officials who slow the fleet down.
characters.name: Admiral Nguyen

characters.description: A Ganymede boy, the son of a family Prax knows, who suffered from the same kind of immune disorder as Mei and was taken to the same clinic before her. His parents were told he had died.
characters.name: Katoa Merton

characters.description: A researcher on the hybrid program whose capacity for emotional attachment was deliberately removed by a surgical procedure. He discusses experiments performed on children with untroubled professional enthusiasm and cannot understand why anyone objects.
characters.name: Doctor Paolo Cortazar

recaps.ending: On Io, the crew reach Mao's laboratory. Prax finds Mei alive, still early enough in the process to be saved, and Amos gets her out; Katoa and the other children who went before her cannot be recovered. Bobbie fights one of the hybrid creatures on the moon's surface in powered armor and destroys it. Nguyen's ship launches a swarm of hybrid-carrying missiles at Earth, and the Rocinante and the gathered fleets, coordinated by Avasarala, destroy them before they reach the planet. Nguyen is broken and arrested, Jules-Pierre Mao is taken into custody, and Errinwright, exposed as the man inside the UN who armed the program, is removed and disgraced, leaving Avasarala with far more power than she had. Doctor Cortazar is captured alive and his research falls into UN hands, which is its own unfinished problem. Prax and Mei are reunited, Bobbie ends up with no service to return to and a place among Avasarala's people, and the Rocinante crew survive intact with Holden somewhat restored to himself. In the closing days, the protomolecule on Venus finishes whatever it has been building: a vast structure lifts off the planet, crosses the solar system, and comes to rest far beyond the orbit of Uranus, where it begins assembling an enormous ring.
recaps.in_short: Eighteen months after Eros, a monstrous figure that survives hard vacuum unarmored destroys a Martian marine patrol on Ganymede, and the resulting battle wrecks the moon that feeds the outer planets. Gunnery Sergeant Bobbie Draper, the only survivor, is sent to Earth to testify and, when her account is suppressed, allies herself with UN official Chrisjen Avasarala, who is hunting whoever is still working with the protomolecule. On Ganymede, botanist Prax Meng searches for his young daughter Mei, taken by her doctor, and joins James Holden and the Rocinante when they arrive to investigate. The threads converge: the industrialist Jules-Pierre Mao, protected by figures inside the UN government, has been using children with immune disorders to grow protomolecule-human hybrids as weapons. Avasarala is lured aboard Mao's ship and effectively held prisoner until Bobbie fights their way out to the Rocinante. The crew track the program to Io, rescue Mei, destroy a hybrid, and stop a missile launch aimed at Earth. Mao and his backers fall; Avasarala rises. On Venus, the protomolecule finishes its work, leaves the planet, and builds an enormous ring beyond the orbit of Uranus.

recaps.text: Previously: an ice hauler was destroyed in the Belt to provoke a war, and the accusation broadcast by its surviving officer, James Holden, nearly set Earth, Mars and the Belt against one another. The real cause was a corporation, Protogen, testing an alien artifact recovered from Saturn's moon Phoebe. The protomolecule was deliberately released on Eros Station and killed its roughly one and a half million residents as an instrumented experiment. Holden and his crew, engineer Naomi Nagata, mechanic Amos Burton and pilot Alex Kamal, came through it with a captured Martian corvette, the Rocinante, and an alliance with Fred Johnson, the former UN colonel who leads the Outer Planets Alliance from Tycho Station. Ceres detective Miller, obsessed with a missing woman named Julie Mao, found her dead of the protomolecule on Eros and later found that her surviving mind was steering the infected station toward Earth. He rode the rock down into Venus with her and died there, stopping it. The war was averted and Protogen destroyed, but the protomolecule is now growing on the surface of Venus, out of anyone's reach and visibly changing, and no government can tell what it is doing. About eighteen months have passed. Earth and Mars remain armed and suspicious of each other, and the Belt is stronger and more organized than before.

On Ganymede, the agricultural moon that feeds the outer planets, Martian and United Nations garrisons watch each other across a demilitarized line. Gunnery Sergeant Bobbie Draper's Martian patrol is destroyed by a single humanoid figure that crosses open ground without a vacuum suit and tears through powered armor; she alone survives. The exchange of fire between the fleets above shatters the moon's mirror array and its growing domes, and Ganymede begins to starve. James Holden and the Rocinante are working for Fred Johnson in the Belt, hunting pirates, and Holden has grown harder and quicker to shoot than the man who once broadcast everything he knew. On Ganymede, the botanist Prax Meng learns that his four-year-old daughter Mei was collected from her daycare by her doctor hours before the fighting started, and that without treatment for her immune disorder she cannot last long. On Earth, the UN official Chrisjen Avasarala works the aftermath and concludes that the incident was engineered, and that the people who arranged it are inside her own government.

Bobbie is sent to Earth as part of a Martian delegation to explain the incident, and when her account of the unarmored figure is edited out of her testimony she understands that her own government would rather bury it than admit what is loose. Avasarala, who suspects the same thing from the other side, takes her in. Fred Johnson sends the Rocinante to Ganymede to look into the rumors, and Holden's crew find a moon collapsing into famine, refugees and gang control. Holden meets Prax, learns that Mei was taken by a doctor named Strickland, and begins to suspect that the missing children and the creature that killed Bobbie's platoon are the same story. Avasarala works out that the only private organization capable of continuing protomolecule research is one that already tried, and starts looking for who is sheltering it.

Following the trail of the missing children, Holden's crew and Prax break into a concealed laboratory beneath Ganymede's surface and find the remains of a program that selected children with compromised immune systems, Mei among them, as candidates for protomolecule work. Something is still alive down there; they meet one of the hybrid creatures and blow it out into vacuum rather than fight it. Prax joins the Rocinante's crew as they leave the dying moon. Avasarala, working through UN channels, becomes certain that the industrialist Jules-Pierre Mao is behind the research and that someone senior on Earth is protecting him, though she cannot yet prove which of her colleagues it is. Bobbie, cut loose by her own chain of command, stays on Earth as Avasarala's liaison and effectively her bodyguard.

Prax records a public appeal for help finding his daughter, and it spreads across the system, turning a private search into a cause with donated money behind it and giving the Rocinante the resources to keep hunting. The crew follow the program's supply lines outward from Ganymede. Avasarala, closing in on Mao, is maneuvered out of her own investigation: she is invited away from Earth on what looks like an opportunity and taken aboard Mao's private ship with Bobbie, where she finds her communications cut and herself a comfortable, well-fed prisoner while the people running the program proceed without her. Meanwhile, on Venus, the protomolecule is visibly reshaping the planet on an enormous scale, and every telescope in the system is pointed at it.

Avasarala learns aboard Mao's ship that her own superior, Sadavir Errinwright, is the man who has been shielding the program, trading UN cover for a weapon he believes Earth must have before Mars does. Admiral Nguyen, hawkish and impatient, commands the naval force protecting the operation. Bobbie takes matters into her own hands, steals a suit of powered armor, and fights the two of them off the ship in a stolen shuttle. They rendezvous with the Rocinante, and the crew, Prax, Bobbie and Avasarala are joined into one improvised alliance: an aging politician with no government behind her, a botanist looking for his daughter, and a corvette with no flag.

The program's location resolves to Io, a moon of Jupiter, where Mao's people have moved the laboratory and the children. Avasarala uses what leverage she still has to turn parts of the UN fleet against Nguyen while Errinwright works to save himself by cutting his patron loose. The Rocinante runs for Io ahead of the warships. Aboard the station there, the hybrids are being finished and loaded, and the researchers regard the children they consumed as materials. Prax, who has spent the whole voyage refusing to believe Mei is dead, prepares to go down with Amos to get her out, knowing the odds and going anyway.

The Rocinante reaches Io ahead of the warships and the crew go down to the laboratory buried under the ice. What they find confirms the worst reading of the evidence: the children taken from Ganymede were raw material, most of them are gone, and the researchers running the program regard the question of consent as a sentimental distraction. Doctor Paolo Cortazar, whose ability to form attachments was surgically removed years ago, explains the work cheerfully to anyone who asks. Elsewhere on the moon the finished hybrids are being loaded into missiles. Above them, Admiral Nguyen's warships hold position while Avasarala, aboard the Rocinante with no office and no title, works the fleets by radio and calls in every debt she has ever been owed, and Errinwright manoeuvres to survive by turning on the patron he protected. Prax, who has refused for the whole voyage to accept that Mei is dead, goes down with Amos to look for her.

On Io the crew reach the laboratory. Prax finds Mei alive and early enough in the process to be saved, and Amos gets her clear; Katoa and the children taken before her cannot be recovered. The researcher Paolo Cortazar, whose ability to care about anyone was surgically removed, is taken alive along with his data. Bobbie meets one of the hybrid creatures on the moon's surface in powered armor and destroys it. Nguyen's ship launches a swarm of missiles carrying hybrids at Earth, and Avasarala, the Rocinante and the fleets she has turned destroy them before they arrive. Nguyen is arrested, Jules-Pierre Mao is taken into custody, and Errinwright is exposed and removed, leaving Avasarala far more powerful than when she started. Prax and Mei are reunited. Then the protomolecule finishes with Venus: a vast structure lifts off the planet, crosses the system, and settles far beyond the orbit of Uranus, where it begins to assemble an enormous ring.

characters.description: A short, plump, unremarkable-looking officer of Britain's security service, badly dressed and easily overlooked. A scholar of seventeenth-century German literature by training, he was recruited into intelligence work before the war and spent it in Germany under cover, running a small network of agents he recruited himself. Back in London he has been reduced to routine vetting and loyalty interviews, work he performs with painstaking care and no appetite for office politics. His marriage to Lady Ann Sercomb has collapsed, which he bears quietly. Patient, courteous and unusually attentive to small inconsistencies, he is the sort of investigator who notices what does not fit and cannot let it alone.
characters.name: George Smiley

characters.description: Smiley's wife, a beautiful and well-connected woman from an aristocratic family, whose marriage to an obscure and dowdy intelligence officer astonished everyone who knew her. She has left him and gone abroad. She is largely absent from the events of the book but is a constant background presence in Smiley's thoughts.
characters.name: Lady Ann Sercomb

characters.description: The senior official who sits between the service and its political masters, a smooth career administrator with no field experience and an unfailing instinct for what will embarrass the department. He values presentation, ministerial comfort and a tidy file above the truth of any particular case, and his handling of the Fennan affair is governed throughout by damage limitation. Smiley regards him with weary contempt.
characters.name: Maston

characters.description: A senior Foreign Office official, Jewish, able and well regarded, who had been a communist sympathiser as an Oxford undergraduate in the 1930s. An anonymous letter revives the old allegation, and Smiley is sent to interview him. The two men talk amicably on a walk in the park, and Smiley leaves convinced there is nothing in it and tells him so.
characters.name: Samuel Fennan

characters.description: Fennan's wife, a small, frail German Jewish refugee who survived the camps and carries their damage in her body and her manner. She lives with her husband in a house at Walliston, sees almost no one, and receives Smiley with a bitter, mocking hostility, treating his questions as another intrusion by a state that has already taken everything from her. Her account of the night of her husband's death does not entirely hold together.
characters.name: Elsa Fennan

characters.description: A younger colleague of Smiley's who has moved into work on East German and satellite intelligence. Loyal, discreet and fond of Smiley, he supplies the departmental knowledge and old files that Smiley can no longer obtain for himself.
characters.name: Peter Guillam

characters.description: A Special Branch inspector close to retirement, thin, dry and precise, who is drawn into Smiley's private investigation. He is a practical policeman with no illusions about official reticence, willing to do legwork the service will not authorise, and he becomes Smiley's most useful ally.
characters.name: Mendel

characters.description: The disreputable proprietor of a Battersea car-hire business, a heavy drinker who rents out vehicles without asking questions and keeps deliberately vague records. He is the one lead Smiley can follow to the fair-haired foreigner who has been using one of his cars.
characters.name: Adam Scarr

characters.description: A German whom Smiley recruited and ran as an agent during the war: lame, physically imposing, formidably intelligent and, at that time, entirely committed to the fight against the Nazis. Smiley thought of him as his best and most difficult pupil, and the two men parted with real affection. He has since made a career in East German intelligence.
characters.name: Dieter Frey

characters.description: A fair-haired, cold-mannered East German operative working in London under commercial cover. He does the practical and violent work of the network he serves, efficiently and without evident feeling, and disposes of anyone who becomes a liability to it.
characters.name: Hans-Dieter Mundt

recaps.ending: Smiley induces Elsa Fennan to send a message that will bring her controller to a meeting. Dieter Frey does not come himself: Mundt murders her at the theatre where the exchanges had been made, removing the last witness who could name the network. Smiley picks up the trail the same night and confronts Dieter on a river bridge in dense fog. They fight, and Dieter, who has the advantage and could kill him, recognises his old case officer and lets go; he falls into the water and drowns. Mundt is already out of the country and escapes to East Germany unpunished. Elsa and Samuel Fennan are both dead, and the service accepts a version of events that spares it embarrassment: Maston can present the case as closed and the department as blameless. Smiley, who has resigned, takes no satisfaction from having been right. He is left with the knowledge that he killed a man he had made, and that the loyalties on which his profession rests are indistinguishable in kind from those of the other side. Convalescing and adrift, he receives word from Ann and leaves England to go to her, his return to the service unresolved.
recaps.in_short: George Smiley, an unassuming officer of Britain's security service, conducts a routine loyalty interview with the Foreign Office official Samuel Fennan after an anonymous letter revives his student communism. Days later Fennan is found shot at home beside a typed suicide note blaming the interview. Smiley's superior wants the affair buried, but details refuse to fit: an early morning telephone call Fennan himself had booked, his widow Elsa's shifting account, and a friendly letter Fennan had posted to Smiley before he died. Working outside the service with the police inspector Mendel and his colleague Peter Guillam, Smiley traces a hired car to a Battersea garage and a fair-haired foreigner, and uncovers a courier routine run through a suburban theatre. The material reaching Moscow was too poor to have been chosen by Fennan: the agent was Elsa, recruited by Dieter Frey, a German whom Smiley himself had recruited and run during the war. Fennan had discovered her and meant to tell Smiley. Elsa is murdered to silence her; Smiley kills Dieter in the fog on the Thames, and Dieter's gunman, Mundt, escapes to East Germany.

recaps.text: George Smiley is a middle-aged, deliberately inconspicuous officer of Britain's security service, a former academic who ran agents in Germany during the war and now handles routine vetting. His wife, Lady Ann Sercomb, has left him. An anonymous letter alleges that Samuel Fennan, a senior Foreign Office official, was a communist at Oxford in the 1930s, and Smiley interviews him informally on a walk in the park, decides there is nothing in the allegation and effectively tells him so. Two days later Fennan is found shot dead in his house at Walliston, with a typed note blaming the interview for ending his career. Maston, the department's political head, is concerned chiefly with the scandal and expects Smiley to close the matter quietly. Visiting the widow, Elsa Fennan, a frail concentration camp survivor who receives him with open hostility, Smiley is interrupted by a telephone call from the exchange: an eight-thirty morning call had been booked for that day. Elsa says she ordered it herself. Smiley does not believe a man who intends to shoot himself that night would want waking, and the explanation she gives sits badly with everything else about her.

Smiley reports his doubts and is told, in effect, to drop them: Maston wants a suicide caused by nothing the department did, and treats Smiley's inconvenient detail as a personal failing. The quarrel is bitter and unresolved. Smiley continues privately. He enlists Mendel, a Special Branch inspector near retirement who is willing to do the observation and enquiry that no one will now authorise, and draws on his colleague Peter Guillam for departmental knowledge of East German operations. A letter from Fennan himself arrives, posted before his death, warm in tone and proposing a further meeting, which is not the act of a man about to kill himself. Small facts accumulate around the widow: her account of the evening does not match the timetable, a strange car has been seen near the house, and her regular attendance at a suburban repertory theatre appears to be more than a habit. Elsa, questioned again, is by turns contemptuous and frightened, and answers with the practised evasions of someone who has been schooled.

The car seen near the Fennan house is traced to Adam Scarr, a drunken Battersea garage owner who hires vehicles out without records. Scarr admits, for money, that the man using it is a fair-haired foreigner he knows only by a nickname and who pays generously in cash. Before the lead can be developed further, Smiley is attacked at his own front door and left seriously injured; he wakes in hospital with time to think. The attack settles the question: this is not an investigation into a suicide but into an active intelligence network operating in London, one which now regards Smiley as dangerous. Maston's response is to seal the case off. Rather than take part in a whitewash, Smiley resigns from the service, which leaves him free to pursue the matter as a private citizen with Mendel and Guillam helping him unofficially.

Adam Scarr, the one man who could describe the fair-haired foreigner, is found dead, which closes that line of enquiry and confirms how thorough the opposition is. Working from outside, Smiley reconstructs how the network operated. The suburban theatre was the exchange point: identical cases were swapped there under cover of a regular audience, so that the courier and the source never had to meet. He also revisits the question of what was actually passed to Moscow. Fennan had access to material of real importance, but what left the house was second-rate, badly chosen and unsystematic, the kind of selection made by someone who could only take what happened to come home in a briefcase. The inefficiency is the proof: the source was not Fennan at all. Elsa, embittered by what was done to her in the camps and persuaded that she was serving peace rather than a foreign state, had been recruited and run for years. Fennan, Smiley now believes, had discovered it. The anonymous denunciation and the interview gave him his opening, and the morning call was booked so that he could telephone Smiley and tell him everything before he lost his nerve.

The controller behind the network is Dieter Frey, a German whom Smiley recruited, trained and ran during the war and remembers with something close to love: lame, brilliant, and now a senior officer of East German intelligence. His practical man in London is Hans-Dieter Mundt, the fair-haired foreigner from the garage, who killed Fennan, staged the suicide, attacked Smiley and disposed of Scarr. Smiley persuades Elsa to send a message arranging a meeting, intending to take Dieter. Instead Mundt goes to the theatre and murders her there among the audience. Smiley pursues Dieter through fog to a bridge over the Thames, where the two men fight. Dieter gets his hands to Smiley's throat, recognises the man who made him and releases his grip rather than kill him, and goes into the river. Mundt has already left the country.

With both Fennans dead, Dieter drowned and Mundt safely back in East Germany, the case is closed on terms that suit everyone official. The department can record a resolved security matter without conceding that a suicide it had accepted was a murder, and Maston is spared. Smiley takes no credit and wants none. Having resigned, he is left to weigh what the affair cost: a man killed for trying to tell the truth, a damaged woman used and then murdered by the people who recruited her, and an agent of his own making dead by his hand. He recognises that Dieter's fanaticism and his own service differ less in method than in the aims they serve, and that Dieter, at the end, was the one who declined to kill. Convalescent, alone and without a profession, Smiley receives word from Ann and leaves England to join her abroad, the future of both his marriage and his career unsettled.

characters.description: The unnamed observer who attends the sale of a celebrated courtesan's possessions and buys her copy of Manon Lescaut. His curiosity brings him into contact with Armand Duval, whose account of Marguerite Gautier's final years becomes the main narrative.
characters.name: The narrator

characters.description: A famous young Parisian courtesan whose elegance, extravagant habits, and customary bouquet of camellias made her widely known. She has recently died of consumption when the narrator first learns of her, and the auction of her belongings exposes how quickly fashionable society has reduced her life to gossip and objects for sale.
characters.name: Marguerite Gautier

characters.description: A young man who arrives distraught after Marguerite's auction and seeks the inscribed book bought by the narrator. His grief is plainly personal, and he becomes the narrator's friend before explaining the history of his love for Marguerite.
characters.name: Armand Duval

characters.description: Marguerite's worldly friend and neighbor, familiar with the practical arrangements and financial pressures of Parisian society. She helps Armand gain entry to Marguerite's circle and often acts as an intermediary between the lovers.
characters.name: Prudence Duvernoy

characters.description: A sociable acquaintance of both Armand and Marguerite who helps bring them together in Paris. He belongs comfortably to the theatrical and fashionable world surrounding Marguerite without sharing Armand's intense attachment.
characters.name: Gaston Rieux

characters.description: Marguerite's loyal maid, responsible for the household's daily routines and for caring for her mistress during bouts of illness. Her position gives her a close view of Marguerite's private suffering behind her public life.
characters.name: Nanine

characters.description: A wealthy older admirer who supports Marguerite and treats her with paternal concern, partly because she resembles his dead daughter. His money offers security but also imposes conditions on how she may live.
characters.name: The Duke

characters.description: A wealthy young man accepted in Marguerite's established social circle. His ability to pay for access to that world makes him a source of jealousy for Armand and a reminder of the arrangements on which Marguerite has depended.
characters.name: Baron de Varville

characters.description: Armand's respectable, protective father. Alarmed by his son's attachment to Marguerite, he comes to intervene with the authority of family duty and conventional society behind him.
characters.name: Monsieur Duval

characters.description: Armand's younger sister, whose prospects for a socially approved marriage become entangled with the Duval family's fear of scandal. She is chiefly present through the obligations others invoke on her behalf.
characters.name: Blanche Duval

characters.description: Another courtesan in Marguerite's Parisian circle. Armand turns to her after his break with Marguerite, drawing Olympe into a campaign meant to provoke and wound his former lover.
characters.name: Olympe

recaps.ending: While Armand is away, Marguerite's illness worsens amid debt and abandonment. Her letters record that she still loves him and hopes for his return, but he learns the truth too late: she dies with only a few loyal attendants near her, and her possessions are seized and sold. Armand returns after her death, visits her grave, and has her body moved so he can see her once more, an experience that leaves him physically and emotionally broken. Monsieur Duval finally confirms that Marguerite left Armand only because he had appealed to her to protect the family's reputation and Blanche's marriage. Armand is left knowing that the apparent betrayal for which he punished Marguerite was an act of sacrifice. He gives the narrator her portrait and preserves her memory, while the narrator closes the account by recognizing both Marguerite's generosity and the cruelty of the social judgment that isolated her.
recaps.in_short: After the death of Marguerite Gautier, a celebrated Parisian courtesan, an unnamed narrator meets the grieving Armand Duval and hears their history. Armand had admired Marguerite from afar, then became her lover despite her illness, debts, and dependence on wealthy patrons. She returned his love and left Paris with him for a quieter life in the country. Armand's father secretly persuaded her that their relationship would disgrace the Duval family and prevent Armand's sister from marrying. Marguerite sacrificed her happiness and made Armand believe she had chosen a richer lover. Not knowing her reason, he retaliated publicly and then left France. Marguerite's consumption and financial troubles overtook her; she died alone before Armand returned. Her letters and his father's confession reveal the truth, leaving Armand to mourn a woman whom society treated as disreputable but whose final choice was selfless.

recaps.text: An unnamed narrator attends the auction of the belongings of Marguerite Gautier, a young Parisian courtesan recently dead of consumption. Her rooms attract fashionable onlookers who treat the sale as entertainment. The narrator buys a copy of Manon Lescaut because of its handwritten dedication. Soon afterward, a distressed young man named Armand Duval asks about the book and explains that he gave it to Marguerite. Moved by his grief, the narrator lets him have it and befriends him. After visiting Marguerite's grave and arranging for her remains to be transferred, Armand falls ill. When he recovers enough to speak, he offers to tell the narrator how he knew her.

Armand explains that he first saw Marguerite in fashionable Parisian venues and became fascinated by her. During one of her serious illnesses he repeatedly asked after her without leaving his name. Much later, their mutual acquaintances Gaston Rieux and Prudence Duvernoy bring him into Marguerite's company. Her lively public manner initially makes light of his devotion, but she is touched to learn that he was the anonymous visitor who cared about her health. When a violent coughing fit exposes how fragile she is, Armand urges her to protect herself and declares his love. Marguerite allows the affair to begin, though she warns him that her life, debts, and other admirers cannot simply disappear. Armand accepts her conditions while already struggling with jealousy.

Armand and Marguerite grow genuinely attached, but their happiness is strained by the practical structure of her life. A wealthy duke and Baron de Varville help sustain expenses that Armand cannot meet, and he repeatedly mistakes Marguerite's financial dependence for indifference. Reconciliations follow their quarrels, and she eventually chooses a quieter life with him at Bougival outside Paris. In the country her health and spirits improve, and the couple live with an ease neither found in Paris. Armand discovers, however, that Marguerite has been selling possessions and taking on losses to preserve their household. His attempt to settle matters with his own limited fortune reveals how precarious their retreat remains.

Monsieur Duval confronts Armand and demands that he end a relationship he regards as ruinous. Armand refuses, convinced of Marguerite's sincerity. His father then meets Marguerite privately and appeals to her on different grounds: public knowledge of the affair threatens the respectable marriage planned for Armand's innocent sister, Blanche. Marguerite agrees to give Armand up without revealing why. She returns to Paris and resumes contact with Varville, leaving a letter that makes her departure appear voluntary and mercenary. Armand is devastated and interprets the evidence as proof that her promises were false. He leaves with his father, unaware that Marguerite has surrendered the life she wanted in order to protect his family.

Back in Paris, Armand seeks revenge instead of an explanation. He begins appearing with Olympe, a courtesan in the same circle, and uses public encounters to make Marguerite jealous. Marguerite begs him to stop and, during a private reunion, admits that she still loves him but says she is bound by a promise she cannot disclose. Armand briefly believes they may be reconciled, only to find her gone again. In anger he sends her money as if paying for their night together, humiliating her and confirming the harshest terms society places on her. He then leaves France. Marguerite, already gravely ill, loses the protection of former patrons and faces mounting debts while still following news of Armand.

Marguerite's final letters reveal a rapid decline marked by illness, creditors, and the disappearance of most of her social circle. She hopes Armand will return and learns that Monsieur Duval has promised to tell him the truth, but she dies before seeing him again. Her belongings are auctioned to satisfy her debts. Armand returns too late, reads the record of her last days, and learns from his father that Marguerite abandoned him only after being asked to save Blanche's marriage and the Duval name from scandal. His own retaliation now appears as punishment inflicted on someone who was protecting his family. He visits Marguerite's grave, preserves her portrait, and entrusts her story to the narrator, who presents her not as the role Paris assigned her but as a woman capable of loyal love and costly sacrifice.

characters.description: The elder Dragna daughter, cautious to the point of paralysis, who has spent her life shielding her reckless younger sister from their father. She experiences emotions as colors, which makes other people's moods vivid to her and her own difficult to hide. For years she has written to Legend, master of the traveling performance called Caraval, asking for tickets. By the time an answer arrives she has been promised in an arranged marriage to a count she has never met, and she has decided that the wedding, not the game, is how she will get herself and her sister off the island.
characters.name: Scarlett Dragna

characters.description: Scarlett's younger sister, impulsive where Scarlett is careful, and unwilling to accept the marriage her sister has arranged both their lives around. She takes risks their father punishes them both for, has attached herself to a sailor named Julian, and is the one who forces the trip to Caraval when the long-awaited tickets finally arrive.
characters.name: Donatella Dragna

characters.description: Governor of the island of Trisda and the sisters' father. He rules his household by violence and has learned that the surest way to control either daughter is to hurt the other one, which keeps Scarlett obedient without his having to touch her. He has arranged Scarlett's marriage for his own advantage and treats disobedience as a debt to be collected.
characters.name: Governor Marcello Dragna

characters.description: A sailor Tella has taken up with, dark-haired and easy with a lie, who offers the sisters passage to the island where Caraval is staged. He is more capable, and far better informed about the game, than a passing sailor has any reason to be, and he consistently avoids saying anything true about himself.
characters.name: Julian

characters.description: The master of Caraval, a performance game staged once a year that is half theater and half wager. Nobody outside his company claims to know his face or his real name; he is known through his letters, his performers, and the stories that have collected around the game. Scarlett has written to him for years, and the reply that finally comes sets the whole book in motion.
characters.name: Legend

characters.description: Scarlett's betrothed, a wealthy man from beyond Trisda whom her father chose and whom she has never met. His letters are courteous, and Scarlett has staked her entire plan for herself and Tella on the marriage being an escape rather than another cage.
characters.name: The Count

characters.description: The sisters' mother, who left Trisda when they were children and never came back. No one has explained why. Her disappearance marks both daughters differently: Scarlett has given up on her, and Tella has not.
characters.name: Paloma Dragna

characters.description: A tall, heavily tattooed young man Scarlett meets inside Caraval, unhurried and hard to read. He knows the game's streets and its rules far better than a first-time player would, and Scarlett cannot tell whether he is a competitor, a performer, or something arranged for her benefit.
characters.name: Dante

characters.description: A tattooed fortune-teller working inside Caraval, who reads cards for players willing to pay his price. What he offers is presented as part of the show, and Scarlett has no way to judge how much of it is meant to be true.
characters.name: Nigel

characters.description: A player who is compiling an illustrated history of Caraval and who trades in stories rather than coin. She is willing to help Scarlett, but only in exchange for something she can use, and her interest is in the game's legend rather than in Scarlett's sister.
characters.name: Aiko

recaps.ending: Caraval closes with Scarlett named the winner, and then she learns that almost everything she suffered through the last five nights was staged. Donatella is alive: she had agreed with Legend to play the missing prize and to fake her own fall, and she never told her sister. Julian is alive too, a Caraval performer who had been working the game from the moment he turned up on Trisda. Scarlett has to set the losses she genuinely paid for - secrets, memories, days of her life - against a performance everyone but her knew was a performance, and being told the deaths were not real does not undo her anger at either of them. She is granted the winner's wish. The sisters leave the isle, beyond their father's reach for the moment, and Scarlett and Julian part without resolving what is between them. The closing pages reveal what Tella's cooperation cost: she had made a bargain with a stranger who promised her word of Paloma, the mother who abandoned them, and the debt is still owed. The next Caraval is announced for the capital of the Meridian Empire, which is where she will have to settle it.
recaps.in_short: Scarlett Dragna and her younger sister Donatella grow up on the island of Trisda under a violent father, sustained by their grandmother's stories about Caraval, a performance game staged once a year by a showman known only as Legend. Days before Scarlett's arranged wedding, the tickets she has been begging for finally arrive, and Tella and a sailor named Julian get her onto a boat to the island where the game is played. There Tella is taken and made the prize: whoever finds her first wins a wish, and Scarlett has five nights. She buys clues with secrets, memories and days of her life, is told constantly that nothing inside Caraval is real, and finds the costs are real anyway. Her father follows her into the game, Julian proves to be a Caraval performer rather than a stranger, and before the last night is over Scarlett has watched both of them die. When the game closes she learns the deaths were staged and both are alive. She wins - and the final pages reveal what Tella traded for her part in it.

recaps.text: Scarlett Dragna lives on Trisda, an island in the Conquered Isles, with her younger sister Donatella and their father, Governor Marcello Dragna, who keeps his daughters in line by hurting one to punish the other. Both girls grew up on their grandmother's stories about Caraval, a performance game staged once a year by a showman called Legend, and Scarlett has spent years writing to him for tickets. She has since been promised in marriage to a count she has never met, and she has decided the wedding is how she will get herself and Tella off the island for good. Then the tickets arrive - three of them. Tella, who has taken up with a sailor named Julian, is determined to go. Scarlett refuses, terrified of what their father will do if they are caught, but Tella and Julian get her aboard a boat regardless, and she wakes at sea, already being carried toward the island where the game is held.

They reach Isla de los Suenos. Caraval turns out to be an entire enclosed quarter of shops, streets and canals that opens only at night, staffed by performers and played by invited guests who are told repeatedly that nothing inside it is real. Before Scarlett can find her sister, Tella is taken: she has been made the object of the game, and the player who finds her first wins the prize, a wish. Scarlett is given five nights, warned that the game ends whether or not she has finished, and given the first clue. Julian stays with her and installs them both at an inn, where they are registered as a married couple so that Scarlett can move through the game without questions. Scarlett wants nothing from Caraval except her sister back and a boat home before her father discovers where they have gone.

The first night of the game. Scarlett follows the clue into Caraval's shops, where nothing is bought with money: the price is a secret, a memory, or a day of her life, and she pays. She is given a dress that changes to suit whatever she needs it to be. Other players are hunting Tella too, and the performers are impossible to tell from the guests. Julian proves to know the game's geography and its rules far better than a sailor should, and deflects every question about how. Scarlett, who sees other people's feelings as colors, spends the night pulled between playing to win and running before the whole thing costs her more than she can afford.

The second night takes Scarlett deeper. She trades away more of herself for information and starts to doubt the rule she has been given about nothing here being real: the injuries, the debts and the losses are real enough to her. Julian's connection to Caraval becomes undeniable - he is not a stranger who happened to have a boat - and Scarlett cannot work out which of his kindnesses were arranged in advance. Meanwhile the days are running down toward the wedding she is supposed to be at, and her father is not a man who lets a daughter simply disappear.

Scarlett loses time to the game and comes back to herself with a stretch of it simply gone. The other players - among them a tattooed young man called Dante, a fortune-teller called Nigel, and Aiko, who is compiling a history of Caraval and will trade help for a story - are further ahead than she is, and each of them wants something from her. Julian's history with Legend's company comes further into the open. The clues keep leading Scarlett toward her sister and, at the same time, further into a performance she cannot see the edges of.

Scarlett's father reaches the island and finds her inside the game, and the violence she fled follows her into it. In the confrontation Julian is gravely hurt, and Scarlett is left believing he is dead. She is now alone, out of allies, and nearly out of nights, and the distinction Legend insisted on - that Caraval is only a performance - has stopped meaning anything to her. She keeps following the clues because finding Tella is no longer about winning a wish.

On the last night Scarlett reaches the end of the clues and finds her sister, too late to change anything: Tella falls to her death in front of her. The game ends with Scarlett declared the winner of a prize she no longer has any use for.

After Caraval closes, Scarlett learns that the deaths she watched were part of the performance. Tella is alive; she had made her own arrangement with Legend, agreeing to play the missing prize and to stage her fall. Julian is alive too, a Caraval performer who had been in the game since before it started, including on Trisda. Scarlett spent five nights paying real prices for a game she was told was not real, and the revelation that her sister was complicit does not simply resolve into relief. She is granted the winner's wish. The sisters leave the isle with Julian and out of their father's reach, with a great deal unsettled between all three of them.

The final pages show what Tella's part in the game actually cost. She had bargained with a stranger who promised her word of their mother, Paloma, who left Trisda when they were children, and what Tella owes in return has not yet been paid. The next Caraval is announced for Valenda, the capital of the Meridian Empire, which is where the debt will come due.

characters.description: The Belgian detective, invited to a dinner whose host promises to display his private collection of people who have killed without being caught. Poirot distrusts both the boast and the host's taste for dangerous effects, but accepts and becomes one of four investigators studying the same closed circle.
characters.name: Hercule Poirot

characters.description: A wealthy collector of curiosities, secrets, and dangerous acquaintances. He enjoys making people uncomfortable and claims he can recognise those who have escaped justice. His dinner party places four investigators and four guests with shadowed pasts at separate bridge tables.
characters.name: Mr Shaitana

characters.description: A successful writer of detective stories, energetic, imaginative, and inclined to prefer dramatic theories to ordinary facts. Shaitana invites her as one of his four representatives of detection, and she conducts her own inquiries among the women connected with the suspects.
characters.name: Ariadne Oliver

characters.description: A senior Scotland Yard officer whose solid manner conceals a patient understanding of people. He represents official police work at Shaitana's dinner and coordinates the inquiry without dismissing Poirot's less conventional questions.
characters.name: Superintendent Battle

characters.description: A British officer whose work has taken him through military and intelligence circles abroad. Cool, discreet, and accustomed to judging danger, he is the fourth investigator at the dinner and follows the international histories behind the guests.
characters.name: Colonel Race

characters.description: A fashionable physician with a large practice, an easy bedside manner, and the confidence of a man used to being welcomed into private homes. He plays bridge boldly and brings the same expansive good humour to Shaitana's dinner.
characters.name: Dr Geoffrey Roberts

characters.description: An elegant widow and exceptionally strong bridge player, composed, intelligent, and unsentimental. She remembers every card and makes few unnecessary statements.
characters.name: Mrs Lorrimer

characters.description: A young woman of modest means who shares a cottage with her friend Rhoda Dawes. Shy and anxious under questioning, she has worked as a companion and carries a strong fear that an incident from an earlier household may be brought into the open.
characters.name: Anne Meredith

characters.description: An explorer and former army officer, quiet, self-contained, and more comfortable with action than explanation. His reserve gives Shaitana ample opportunity for insinuation without immediate contradiction.
characters.name: Major John Despard

characters.description: Anne Meredith's practical, outspoken housemate and friend. She is less easily intimidated than Anne and helps Mrs Oliver reconstruct the circumstances of Anne's former employment. Her frankness also attracts Major Despard's attention.
characters.name: Rhoda Dawes

characters.description: The widow of an explorer who died during an expedition with Major Despard. Her account of her marriage and of Despard's conduct complicates the version suggested by Shaitana's insinuations.
characters.name: Mrs Luxmore

characters.description: A former domestic servant in the household of one of Dr Roberts's patients. Her recollection of illness, treatment, and household tensions gives Battle a view of an old death from below stairs.
characters.name: Elsie Batt

recaps.ending: Poirot identifies Dr Geoffrey Roberts as Shaitana's murderer. During the bridge game Roberts moved about freely as dummy, took a slim dagger from the room, and stabbed the host while the other players were absorbed in their cards. Shaitana had recognised that Roberts had used medical access to remove inconvenient patients in the past. When the inquiry threatened him, Roberts also killed Mrs Lorrimer by injection and arranged the scene as suicide, using her genuine admission about her husband's death to make a false confession to Shaitana's murder seem credible. Poirot breaks him with a manufactured eyewitness and with the contrast between what each player's bridge record shows about temperament and opportunity. The other histories are separated from the present crime. Mrs Lorrimer had killed her husband years earlier but did not kill Shaitana. Major Despard's expedition shooting was an accident he concealed to protect Mrs Luxmore. Anne Meredith caused a former employer's death while hiding theft; when she later tries to drown Rhoda Dawes, Despard rescues Rhoda and Anne herself drowns. Roberts is arrested, while Despard and Rhoda are left free to begin a life together.
recaps.in_short: Mr Shaitana, a collector of dangerous secrets, invites four detectives and four people he believes have killed before without conviction to dinner. While Poirot, Superintendent Battle, Colonel Race, and Ariadne Oliver play bridge in one room, Dr Roberts, Mrs Lorrimer, Major Despard, and Anne Meredith play in another beside their host. Shaitana is stabbed while they play, leaving four suspects who all had opportunity. The investigators reopen the old deaths Shaitana had discovered and study the bridge score for signs of character and movement. Mrs Lorrimer admits killing her husband, then dies after apparently confessing to Shaitana's murder. Poirot proves that Dr Roberts killed both Shaitana and Mrs Lorrimer, having previously exploited his medical position to kill patients. Despard's old shooting was accidental. Anne had caused a former employer's death while concealing theft and later tries to kill Rhoda Dawes, but drowns during the attempt. Roberts is trapped and arrested; Despard and Rhoda survive.

recaps.text: At an exhibition Poirot meets Mr Shaitana, a flamboyant collector who boasts that his finest collection consists of people who have murdered without being caught. Shaitana arranges a dinner for eight guests: four investigators - Poirot, Superintendent Battle, Colonel Race, and detective novelist Ariadne Oliver - and four people whose histories he has privately marked - Dr Roberts, Mrs Lorrimer, Major Despard, and Anne Meredith. After dinner the groups divide into two bridge tables. The investigators play in one room while the other four play near Shaitana, who sits by the fire. At the end of the evening Shaitana is found stabbed with a slender weapon taken from his own collection. Every player at that table had opportunities to leave a seat while acting as dummy, and none admits noticing the crime.

The four investigators divide the work according to their strengths. Battle follows records and witnesses, Race looks into Despard's life abroad, Mrs Oliver approaches the personal circles around Anne and Mrs Lorrimer, and Poirot concentrates on psychology. The bridge score becomes a record of the evening: Mrs Lorrimer played with exceptional control, Roberts took risks, Despard was steady, and Anne became increasingly uncertain. Poirot asks not only who could have crossed the room but who would act suddenly under pressure. Each suspect denies knowing why Shaitana invited them. Early inquiries reveal a questionable death or accident somewhere in each past, but the evidence is too incomplete to show which history Shaitana understood correctly or which guest feared immediate exposure.

Poirot and Battle interview the four separately and reconstruct their lives. Dr Roberts's successful practice gives him access to patients and medicines, though he laughs off gossip around an earlier household. Mrs Lorrimer answers with precision and offers no emotional defence. Anne Meredith is frightened by questions about a former employer and by the possibility that small thefts may be discovered. Major Despard admits that an expedition ended with a man shot but rejects the malicious version of events. Poirot also asks each player what they remember of the room during the game, testing attention rather than demanding a direct accusation. The accounts differ over movements, ornaments, and conversation, while the score sheets continue to show when each person could have left the table unnoticed.

The investigators reach people who can clarify the old cases. Elsie Batt describes the household of one of Dr Roberts's former patients and the medical treatment surrounding a suspicious death. Rhoda Dawes, Anne's confident housemate, helps Mrs Oliver trace the companion position Anne once held and the valuables that disappeared there. Mrs Luxmore gives an account of the South American expedition that does not match the simple suggestion that Despard deliberately killed her husband. These inquiries establish that Shaitana had found genuine secrets, but not all the secrets are equivalent and not every concealment is murder. Poirot becomes increasingly interested in the difference between a person who plans patiently and one who seizes a brief opportunity, because Shaitana's death required both nerve and perfect timing.

Mrs Lorrimer privately admits to Poirot that she killed her husband years ago. Soon afterward she is found dead, apparently by her own hand, with a confession that seems to accept responsibility for Shaitana as well. Poirot does not believe the second confession fits either her character or the physical circumstances. Her death removes the strongest bridge player and appears to close the case too efficiently. Meanwhile the histories of Despard and Anne sharpen in different directions, and Rhoda's knowledge places strain on her friendship with Anne. Poirot prepares a trap based on an alleged observer who could have seen into Shaitana's room, while Battle checks the means by which Mrs Lorrimer died. The solution now depends on whether the apparent suicide is accepted as an ending or recognised as another attempt to arrange the table.

Poirot names Dr Geoffrey Roberts as the murderer of both Shaitana and Mrs Lorrimer. Acting as dummy during the bridge game, Roberts could move through the room naturally, take the slim dagger, and stab Shaitana while the others concentrated on their cards. Shaitana knew of earlier deaths in which Roberts had abused the trust and access of a physician. Roberts later injected Mrs Lorrimer and staged her death as suicide, attaching a false confession to the true fact that she had killed her husband years before. Poirot's supposed eyewitness is a trap that forces Roberts to reveal himself, while the bridge record supports the opportunity and temperament. The other secrets are disentangled: Despard accidentally shot Mr Luxmore and concealed the circumstances to protect Mrs Luxmore; Anne caused a former employer's death while covering theft. Anne then tries to drown Rhoda, but Despard saves Rhoda and Anne drowns. Roberts is arrested, and Despard and Rhoda are left together.

characters.description: Now a rising star of the crawl, Carl enters the third floor having chosen the Primal race, which leaves him looking human, and the Compensated Anarchist class, which leans into his gift for improvised explosives. Still shoeless and pantsless by the game's design, he fights with his fists, his feet, and increasingly elaborate bombs, and his instinct to protect other crawlers and even non-player characters keeps dragging him into quests he never wanted.
characters.name: Carl

characters.description: Carl's talking Persian cat and party leader. Following advice from the talk-show host Odette, she keeps her Cat race and takes the Former Child Actor class, a choice that comes with a manager: Mordecai, now magically bound to appear in any safe room she enters. Vain, theatrical, and fiercely attached to Carl and her pet dinosaur Mongo, she grows into a genuinely dangerous spellcaster on this floor while remaining convinced the whole dungeon is beneath her.
characters.name: Princess Donut

characters.description: The pair's guide, now formally bound to Donut as her class-granted manager, summoned into every safe room the party enters whether he likes it or not. He greets the arrangement by drinking heavily, but his encyclopedic knowledge of the dungeon's floors, monsters, and unwritten rules makes him indispensable, and beneath the bitterness he plainly cares what happens to them.
characters.name: Mordecai

characters.description: Donut's devoted pet dinosaur, brought down from the second floor. Young, loud, and violent in his mistress's defense, he serves as the party's mount and shock troop, and Donut's willingness to risk her own life for him becomes a point of friction between her and Carl.
characters.name: Mongo

characters.description: An Elite non-player character of the third floor: a tattooed, half-naiad, half-elf tsarina of overwhelming supernatural charisma whose moving tattoos crawl across her skin. She binds Carl into her quest against the corrupted remains of a traveling circus, and her scripted tragedy raises uncomfortable questions about how real the dungeon's people are.
characters.name: Signet

characters.description: The ringmaster of a once-traveling circus, now a parasitic vine creature presiding over a corrupted troupe of undead performers. He is the monstrous heart of the quest Signet forces on Carl, and confronting him requires walking into the big top itself rather than burning it down.
characters.name: Ringmaster Grimaldi

characters.description: The severe gatekeeper who controls all access to Featherfall, the magistrate of the settlement where Carl and Donut base themselves. The party's investigation into the death of the goblin GumGum runs straight into her obstruction, and getting past her desk becomes a quest problem in its own right.
characters.name: Miss Quill

characters.description: A crawler and friend of the Amazon crawler Hekla, struggling with her chosen Doppelganger race: reshaping her body is slow and painful, and she reverts to her true form when she sleeps.
